questions.question: In a graph G = (V, E), what does V stand for?
questions.rationale: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices and a set of edges joining pairs of them; the degree of a vertex counts the edges that touch it.

questions.question: How much space does an adjacency list need?
questions.rationale: An adjacency list stores one neighbour list per vertex for O(V + E) space, which is why it is the default for sparse real-world graphs.

questions.question: Which data structure powers breadth-first search?
questions.rationale: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to explore level by level — the start, then its neighbours, then their neighbours.

questions.question: On the lesson graph (edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, C–E), what is the BFS visit order from A?
questions.rationale: BFS explores level by level: A first, then its neighbours B and C, then D and E — giving A, B, C, D, E.

questions.question: On the same graph, trying neighbours alphabetically, what is the DFS order from A?
questions.rationale: DFS dives down one branch fully: A to B to D to C, then backtracks to reach E — order A, B, D, C, E.

questions.question: In an unweighted graph, which traversal finds shortest paths?
questions.rationale: BFS reaches every vertex in fewest-edges-first order, so it delivers shortest paths in unweighted graphs; weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

questions.question: Which constraint does Dijkstra's algorithm require?
options: The graph must be a tree
questions.rationale: Dijkstra requires non-negative weights: a negative edge can make an already-settled vertex improvable, breaking the greedy assumption.

questions.question: What does Bellman-Ford offer that Dijkstra does not?
options: It handles negative edges and detects negative cycles
questions.rationale: Bellman-Ford allows negative edges and detects negative cycles in O(V·E) time — slower, but it works when weights can go below zero.

questions.question: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm works by:
options: Growing one tree from a start vertex
Sorting all edges and adding each cheapest edge that does not close a cycle
questions.rationale: Kruskal sorts all edges and adds each cheapest edge that does not close a cycle, using union-find to test for cycles fast.

questions.question: Topological sorting applies to which kind of graph?
questions.rationale: A topological order lists vertices of a DAG so every edge points forward — prerequisites always come before dependents.
